cultivar: Mengshan local landrace plus Fuding Dabai and Mingshan clones such as Mingshan Bai Hao 131
processing: Pan-fired green with repeated rolling: the shoots are fired and rolled three times in alternation (the 'three fires, three rolls' method) so the tender leaf curls tightly and the down is raised, then finished with a gentle drying.
harvest_season: Very early spring thanks to the Sichuan climate: picking can start in late February or early March, with the best bud-and-one-leaf lots in mid-March; it is comfortably pre-Qingming.
appearance_dry: Small, tightly curled, downy twists in silvery green, uniform and fuzzy.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green, bright, with a light haze of down.
appearance_wet: Tiny bud-and-leaf sets, tender and even, yellow-green.
taste_profile: Soft, sweet and fuzzy-textured with fresh bean and a light chestnut note, a touch of orchid, and a quick return of sweetness after a gentle grip.

brewing.notes: Glass or gaiwan at 80 °C. The leaf is tender and downy, so pour water first or down the side of the glass; a short first steep keeps it sweet.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, and because Sichuan starts picking in late February it is one of the first new greens on the market each year, with pre-Qingming lots plentiful rather than scarce. Grades run from special grade (small buds with one leaf, mid-March) downwards; 'Mengding' is the protected name, 'Sichuan Ganlu' from the wider Ya'an area is the cheaper version. Drink within the year, kept cold.
description:
Mengding Gan Lu, 'sweet dew of Mengding', is the signature green of Mengding Mountain in Ya'an, Sichuan, a wet, misty ridge that the Chinese tea world likes to call the oldest cultivated tea garden (the Han-dynasty planting story is a legend, but the gardens are genuinely old). It is a small, curly, downy tea, and the first thing you notice is the softness: the texture is fuzzy and sweet, with none of the sharp edges of the eastern greens.

The curl comes from an unusual amount of rolling. After the first firing the leaf is rolled, fired again, rolled again, and so on, three rounds in all, which tightens the tender shoots into little twists and raises the silvery down. The finishing heat is kept low, so the tea stays pale and fresh rather than toasty.

In the cup you get fresh bean and a hint of chestnut, a little orchid, and above all a quick, clean sweetness that comes back after each sip. It is a gentle three-steep tea. Treat it like Biluochun: 80 °C, water first into the glass if you can, little leaf. Pushed hard it gets grassy rather than bitter, which is a kinder failure mode than most greens.

Sichuan's warm, early spring means Gan Lu is picked from late February, weeks before Hangzhou or Suzhou, and it reaches shops as the first proper new tea of the year. That early date is a feature, not a warning sign, as it would be for Longjing. Grades follow bud size and picking date; the top lots are tiny buds with one leaf from around mid-March. The Mengding name is protected, and tea from the surrounding Ya'an hills is sold more cheaply as Sichuan Ganlu or just 'Ganlu'.

The mountain also makes a flat green (Mengding Shihua) and a yellow tea (Mengding Huangya) from the same material, both worth tasting alongside this one.
history:
The usual story says a Taoist master, Wu Lizhen, planted seven tea bushes on Meng Mountain during the Ganlu era of the Han dynasty (53 to 50 BCE), which would make it the first cultivated tea anywhere. It is a legend, though an old one: the Song emperor Xiaozong gave Wu a posthumous title containing the word Ganlu, 'sweet dew', and the tea's name is traced to it.

The mountain's tribute record is firmer, running from the Tang to the Qing, with monks said to prepare just 360 leaves each spring for the emperor. That tribute was not necessarily this tea, since the best-known Tang listing names Mengding Shihua.

Gan Lu in its present role is fairly recent. Around 1950 the yellow Huang Ya was the mountain's main tea, and Gan Lu has only since moved into first place, now counted as a model of the curled Chinese green.
